passage:
At ten, Jomon told Mummy Farida, "My leaf collection is easy. Ten minutes and it's done." He began the evening before it was due, and the leaves kept tearing, and the glue would not hold. It took him until bedtime, and he cried a little over an empty page for oak.
At fifteen, Jomon had exams in four subjects. On Friday he told his friend Anirban, "I'll finish all of physics revision this weekend." By Sunday night he had done a third of it. The following Friday he said, with the same confidence, "Chemistry, this weekend, whole subject." Again he got through a third. Anirban, walking home with him, said, "Didn't you say that about physics?" Jomon paused. "That was different. Physics is heavier." The next Friday he drew up an identical schedule for biology. Mummy Farida saw the timetable on the wall and did not comment; instead she asked if he wanted her to sit with him on Saturday morning to write down what each chapter really needed. Jomon looked at the empty biology notebook and nodded.

qa.q: In how many subjects did Jomon have exams at fifteen?
qa.a: He had exams in four subjects.

qa.q: What pattern connects the leaf collection at ten with the weekend revision plans at fifteen?
qa.a: Each time Jomon imagines the work will go quickly and pictures the smooth version. The leaves and glue at ten and the third of physics and chemistry at fifteen did not teach him, so he repeated the same schedule for biology.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he cried a little over the empty page for oak?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and disappointed, because the task he expected to be easy was far from done.

qa.q: How could Mummy Farida help Jomon plan the biology revision?
qa.a: She could sit with him and list what each chapter really needs, then check how much of physics and chemistry he actually finished in a weekend.

grounding: A child's belief homework will be quick (3650) and a teen who repeats the same weekend plan for each subject despite missing (7656): one boy over years.
